1.pericope_label: Am I not free, am I not an apostle; ye are the seal of mine apostleship
debates: What order the opening clauses stand in and what the freedom means: Gill reports that the Syriac, Ethiopic, Vulgate and Alexandrian copy put the clause about freedom first and that many interpreters prefer it, the argument then rising from the less to the greater; Ellicott prefers the same order on manuscript grounds and finds the thought grows more naturally out of the preceding chapter; Gill will not fix the sense of the freedom, offering liberty in things indifferent, freedom from the ceremonial law at large, or the right to a maintenance, while Robertson takes it of Mosaic ceremonialism and Wesley reads the clauses as a rising scale

How often Paul saw the Lord: Lightfoot says twice, on the road to Damascus when he was marked out for an apostle and in the trance at Jerusalem when he was marked out for the apostle of the Gentiles, and claims further that he alone among the apostles saw the Lord after the ascension; Robertson gathers half a dozen passages and observes that they qualify him though he was not one of the twelve; Ellicott names three occasions and infers from the unanswered question that the fact was generally admitted

Whether the argument from success proves too much: Calvin alone raises the objection himself, that the same reasoning would serve the false apostles who also gather disciples, and answers that pure doctrine is required before any man may argue from his effect, so that impostors have no ground of congratulation though they deceive nations and kingdoms; Barnes by contrast presses the conversion as absolute proof and irrefragable demonstration without meeting that difficulty
outliers: Chrysostom's account of why the argument stands here, that Paul had promised to eat no flesh for ever and was compelled to show by deeds something he had slighted for his brother's sake, and his escalation that the admirable part is not the abstinence but the habit of it at the cost of much trouble and danger

Calvin's principle that whatever law a man imposes on others he should submit to himself, and his reason for citing past conduct rather than the promise, that a promise for the future might not be believed by all
Henry's pastoral note that it is no strange nor new thing for a minister to meet unkind returns for great good-will and successful service
Clarke's statement of the injustice, that the very thing which was the highest proof of Paul's disinterested benevolence was produced by his opponents as an argument against him

Barnes's reconstruction of the four charges behind the chapter, that Paul had not seen Christ, that he lived unlike the other apostles, that he and Barnabas laboured with their hands, and that his not claiming maintenance showed he knew he had no right to it
Clarke's antiquarian note that the seal was a figure cut in a stone and set in a ring by which letters of credence were stamped, and that the moderns contend in vain to rival the ancient engravers
themes: have I not seen Jesus our Lord

3.pericope_label: My answer to them that examine me; have we not power to eat and drink
debates: Whether the sentence about his defence looks backward or forward: Gill reports that some refer it to the questions following but holds it belongs to what precedes; Clarke attaches it to the two preceding verses and Wesley to what has just been given; Ellicott says flatly that it refers to what has gone before and not to what follows; Robertson alone will have it both ways, referring it to what precedes and to what follows alike

What the sister who is a wife means: Gill calls it a Hebraism answering to the sister-spouse of the Canticles and rejects the reading that makes her a rich woman ministering of her substance, since that would relieve the churches of the very charge Paul is claiming; Ellicott dismisses the same Roman reading because the appeal to Peter makes it inadmissible, and records that the practice growing out of that misapprehension was condemned at the first council of Nicaea; Henry argues from the word for power, which implies authority to require attendance, such as no man has over any but a wife or servant; Clarke takes the verse as decisive against clerical celibacy while noting that Clement of Alexandria said the apostles carried their wives not as wives but as sisters

Whether Paul himself was married: Calvin reports that Eusebius inferred from these words that Paul was married and had left his wife somewhere lest she burden the churches, and denies there is any foundation for it, since he might urge the right without possessing it; Robertson agrees that plainly Paul had no wife at this time
outliers: Robertson's warning that the noun for defence does not carry our sense of apologising, and his aside that the critics at Corinth were investigating Paul with sharp eyes to find faults, as pastors are still kept under the critic's spy-glass

Lightfoot's motive for the whole apology, given by no one else, that Paul was accused of taking maintenance from heathen churches, or watched by cavillers to see whether he would, and turned to mechanic labour to stop the mouths of the Jews who barked against him
Calvin's turn of the argument on the readers, that the Corinthians injure themselves by refusing the acknowledgment, since their faith and his apostleship must stand or fall together

Robertson's observation that this is the first mention of Barnabas since the dispute at Antioch and that it is made in good spirit, with the suggestion that the two received no help on the first journey and Paul had no financial aid until Philippi

Clarke's excursus into English usage, that a clergyman's provision came to be called a living and his work the cure of souls, whether from the word for care or because the souls are diseased and the minister a physician

Calvin's concession and limitation together, that Peter was acknowledged first among the apostles since every society needs one to preside, but that the pre-eminence was not lordship and the first place in one church is not dominion over the world
themes: my answer to them that examine me
the brethren of the Lord and Cephas

7.pericope_label: Who goeth a warfare at his own charges; thou shalt not muzzle the ox
debates: What the question about the oxen means: Barnes and Wesley supply a word, asking whether God cares for oxen only and whether he has not a further meaning; Clarke turns it into an argument from the lesser to the greater, that God cannot be solicitous for oxen and regardless of man; Ellicott enters the opposite caution, that the words must not be taken as denying the divine regard for the brute creation, which runs through the Mosaic law and appears in the closing question of Jonah, but as stating the ultimate and highest object of God’s love

Clarke’s use of the verse against the decree of reprobation, which no other voice in the chapter follows: God could not reprobate an ox since he careth for oxen, and surely cannot reprobate a man; and to the reply that a man has sinned and an ox cannot, he answers that the decree is supposed to be from eternity, and a man can no more sin before he exists than an ox can when he exists

Why this proof text and not a clearer one: Calvin alone asks why Paul chose the muzzled ox when plainer passages lay to hand, such as the command that the hireling’s wages not remain overnight, and answers that there is more force in this one, since a requirement to care for cattle yields an argument from the less to the greater about the equity God expects among men; Barnes meanwhile guards the inference, that Moses is not being made to speak of the Christian ministry, only that the principle was settled there
outliers: Robertson's derivation of the word for a soldier's pay from a term for cooked meat bought with bread, so that it meant rations before wages, and his note that it is the word used of the wages of sin
Gill's and Calvin's agreement that men have served at their own charges, Gill naming the Habessines and the ancient Romans and dating the senate's act for a stipend before Paul wrote

Ellicott's textual preference for the shorter reading, that the vineyard owner eats his fruit while the keeper of a flock eats of the milk, since a man may eat fruit but is sustained by milk only through selling it

Ellicott's observation that Paul never takes up the Lord's own image of Christ the Shepherd and the Church his flock, with a single exception at Miletus, and does not take it up even here where the word flock stood in his own sentence, whereas it is Peter's favourite image
Robertson's remark that the catalogue of illustrations is proof enough in all conscience and still not enough for churches that starve their pastors in the name of piety

Robertson's description of the threshing-floor, with oxen or donkeys dragging a sledge over the grain as they still do in Andalusia and Palestine, and the hieroglyphic inscription bidding the oxen thresh measures of grain for themselves and measures for their masters
themes: thou shalt not muzzle the ox

10.pericope_label: Saith he it altogether for our sakes; we have not used this power
debates: What the text of the ploughing clause should be: Clarke reports that many of the best manuscripts give simply in hope of partaking and quotes Bishop Pearce that the longer words are superfluous if not wrong, since men do not live in hope to partake of their hope but of what their hope was for, Griesbach having left them out; Calvin describes the same double reading, counts the manuscripts on each side, and then declines to follow his own preference, saying that were he at liberty to choose he would prefer the shorter but that since most Greek manuscripts agree in the other and the meaning is unaffected he has not ventured to alter it

How far the word altogether reaches: Barnes denies flatly that it can mean the law was made solely for ministers, since that would contradict a law which had a real reference to oxen, since the argument does not require it, and since the word may be rendered chiefly or doubtless as elsewhere in Luke and Acts; Gill leans the other way, that God delivered the law not merely for the ox but chiefly for men, citing Jarchi that the ox is named in order to express man

Whether the ploughing and threshing are literal or spiritual: Ellicott says the question has been much discussed and takes them literally, as God’s sanction upon the principle uniting earthly labour with reward, the application to spiritual work following from the less to the greater; Robertson observes what the others miss, that the two halves are not parallel, since the thresher may be the ox but the plougher can hardly be
outliers: Barnes's three grounds for limiting the word altogether, and his parallels for the weaker sense from Luke and Acts
Gill's citation of Jarchi that the ox is named in the law in order to express man, with a second Jewish authority reading the law of the bird's nest the same way

Calvin's anticipation of the cavil that gospel fruit is spiritual and so its ministers should demand nothing carnal, answered from the greater to the less, that in proportion as the soul excels the body does the word excel outward sustenance

Ellicott's ear for a slight touch of sarcasm, since the earlier argument established a labourer's right to payment in kind and Paul now asks only a reward as inferior to his work as carnal things are to spiritual

Gill's expansion of the sowing figure into the parable of the soils, the wayside hearers on whom no impression is made, the stony who show affection without root, the thorny who are at first promising
Robertson's note that the word for hindrance means a cutting in and is very rare, and his judgment that Paul's care to avoid it rather than insist on his rights is an eloquent example for modern men
themes: we have not used this power

13.pericope_label: They which minister about holy things; the Lord ordained; I have used none of these
debates: Who the two classes of ministrants are: Barnes takes the first for the Levites and the second for the priests who offered sacrifice; Clarke widens the first to all the officers, priests and Levites and Nethinim alike, observing that the priests partook of the sacrifices while the rest lived on tithes and first fruits since it was not lawful for them to live on the sacrifices; Ellicott divides by the kind of support rather than the rank; Lightfoot supplies rabbinic detail nobody else has, that among those who wrought in holy things without serving at the altar were the men who picked the worms out of the altar wood, blemished men unfit to minister there but nourished from the consecrated things

What waiting at the altar means: Lightfoot corrects the picture, since none but the king might sit within the court, so that the word means rather besieging the altar, spread everywhere about it, some carrying off ashes, some killing the sacrifice, others sprinkling the blood; the others take the term simply of constant attendance

How the broken sentence of the last verse should be read: Robertson says the tangled syntax reflects the intensity of Paul’s feeling and marks the violent break where the expected infinitive gives way to a bare future, no man shall make my glorying void; Ellicott reports a great variety of readings and sets out more than one reconstruction of the sentence
outliers: Chrysostom's attention to the phrasing, that Paul wrote not that the ministers receive from those who offer but that they eat of the temple, so that neither the receivers may be blamed nor the givers lifted up, and that this indicates their moderation and that it does not behove them to make money or be rich

The agreement of Gill and Ellicott in rejecting outright the reading that the priests meant are those of the heathen temples, which the Ethiopic version suggests and Ellicott calls wholly inadmissible
Ellicott's quotation of Bengel, that if the Mass were a sacrifice Paul would undoubtedly have fitted the second half of his sentence to it
Barnes's limitation of what the ordinance grants, that the word is live and not grow rich, lay up treasures, speculate, or turn merchant or farmer
Clarke's Jewish maxim that the inhabitants of a town where a wise man dwelt should support him because he had forsaken the world's pleasures to study
Henry's definition of the glorying, that it implies nothing of boasting or self-conceit or catching at applause but a high degree of satisfaction and comfort
themes: they which minister about holy things

16.pericope_label: Necessity is laid upon me; what is my reward then
debates: What the word rendered abuse means: Clarke argues that it does not mean abusing but using to the uttermost, exacting everything a man may claim by law, and Robertson agrees so far as the grammar goes, taking the compound in its perfective force as using to the full; Wesley keeps a shade of the older sense and renders it an unseasonable use

How the difficult passage should be construed: Barnes admits the three verses are very difficult and have been very variously understood; Ellicott proposes to remove the question mark altogether and read the last verse as one sentence, asking what reward is to be his which induces him to make the gospel without charge; Clarke will not settle it and prints two other men’s renderings beside his own, from Knatchbull and from Wakefield; Robertson admits the reasoning is not wholly clear and cuts the knot by making the freedom of charge itself the whole reward

Whether the passage establishes works of supererogation: Calvin alone raises the Roman inference, that since Paul might have fulfilled his office by preaching and here adds something over and above, a class of works beyond duty is established, and he refuses it, holding that what is added is not beyond duty but the very willingness without which the duty is not discharged as it should be
outliers: Wesley's observation that Paul speaks here in a manner peculiar to himself, since another might have preached willingly and still received a maintenance, whereas if Paul had received anything he would have called that preaching unwillingly, and another might have used the power without abusing it, whereas Paul would have called his using it at all an abuse
Clarke's double warning, woe to the man who runs when God has not sent him and woe to him who refuses to run or ceases to run when God has sent him

Robertson's turning of the necessity into a compliment, that Paul could do no other and deserves no credit for it, having heard a real call, with the wish that the same were true of every modern preacher
Gill's distinction that Paul might glory before men and against the false teachers but not before God, since the gifts, the light, the courage and the success were all of grace

Clarke's double-edged application, that preachers who insist on their privileges tempt people to think they seek secular goods, and yet the people readiest to think so are those unwilling to grant common necessaries to those who watch over them
Barnes's two guards on the conclusion, that Paul did not give up his support because he had no right to it, and that he does not say others would do well to follow him in it
themes: woe is unto me if I preach not

19.pericope_label: Free from all, servant to all; I am made all things to all men
debates: Who the men without law are, disputed between two voices in the catena itself: Lightfoot raises the question whether the Sadducees or the heathen are meant, tells his reader to inquire, confesses that how Paul could make himself conformable to the heathen is not easy to judge, and allows conformity to the Sadducees in rites but never in their heresy about the resurrection; Clarke names Lightfoot and refuses the suggestion on two grounds, that Paul could expect no success among men who denied the resurrection and a future world, and that among the heathen he might well appear as one who was not a Jew; Gill, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley take the phrase of the heathen without discussion

Who the weak are: Gill and Barnes take them for weak Christians, scrupulous about meats and offended by things lawful in themselves; Ellicott says we can scarcely read it so, since the whole passage treats of classes outside the Church whom Paul hoped to gain, and renders it that he assimilated himself to the weak points rather than the strong points of Jews, proselytes and Gentiles alike

Who the men under the law are: Ellicott makes them proselytes as distinct from Jews by birth; Barnes takes it as another way of naming the same people, perhaps those living in Judea itself; Lightfoot suggests the Jews at large as against the Pharisees in particular, who seemed to subject themselves to the law more than the rest of the nation
outliers: Gill's notice that the word men is not in the original and the phrase may as well be neuter, so that the freedom is from the curse of the moral law and the yoke of the ceremonial, with Barnes and Calvin weighing the same ambiguity and preferring the personal sense

Henry's statement of the paradox, that Paul was free-born and a citizen of Rome and depended on no one, yet was careful to please as a servant is careful to please his master, and made himself a servant that others might be made free

The agreement of Clarke and Ellicott that the clause denying Paul was himself under the law belongs to the text, Clarke listing the uncials and versions behind it and Ellicott ascribing its absence to a copyist's oversight
Robertson's phrase borrowed from Evans, not an outlaw of God but an inlaw of Christ
Ellicott's ear for humility in the close, that the natural climax would have been to win all and that Paul dared not hope for so great a reward, writing instead that he might save some

Cyril's inversion of the phrase, applying it to Christ, who comes in various forms to each man for his profit, a Vine to those who need gladness, a Door to those who would enter, a High Priest to those who must offer prayers, a Sheep to those who have sins, and is made all things to all men while remaining in his own nature what he is
themes: free from all, servant to all
to the Jews as a Jew

23.pericope_label: This I do for the gospel; they which run in a race; temperate in all things
debates: What the word rendered the gospel means in the first verse: Clarke goes further than anyone else and proposes that it should here be rendered the prize or reward, so that Paul does all this for the sake of the prize that he may partake of it with them; Robertson reads the sentence the other way, taking the compound to mean a joint partaker with others and finding in it Paul’s evangelistic passion, that he does not wish to enjoy the gospel just by himself; Barnes and Ellicott keep to the common sense, that Paul hoped to share the salvation he preached

How far the comparison with the race holds: Clarke, Calvin, Wesley and Henry all state the disanalogy, that there only one received the prize though all ran while here all who run may receive it, Henry adding that there should nevertheless be a noble emulation and a glorious contest who shall get first to heaven; Chrysostom alone guards the other flank, warning expressly that the words are not to be taken as though here also only one out of many would be saved, far from it, but as setting forth the exceeding diligence it is our duty to use

What the turn to the games is doing in the argument: Chrysostom reads it as a sharpening of the rebuke, a covert intimation that what the Corinthians counted a mark of perfectness is a superfluous and useless labour, not said out clearly lest they grow insolent, whereas Barnes and Ellicott take it simply as an illustration of self-denial drawn from a spectacle familiar to the readers
outliers: The agreement of Gill, Clarke and Ellicott that the better manuscripts read all things rather than this, Clarke listing the uncials and the Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, Itala, Armenian and Sahidic behind it

Ellicott's account of the games themselves, that none but freemen could enter, that competitors had to satisfy the officers of ten months' training and thirty days at the gymnasium, that a herald proclaimed each man's name and country, and that the victor returning home entered his native town through a breach made in the walls
Gill's note that the Corinthians were themselves presidents of these games, so that the allusion needed no explaining
The divergence in measuring the course, Gill making it six hundred and twenty-five feet where Robertson makes it six hundred and six and three quarters

Clarke's long quotation of Epictetus on the cost of an Olympic victory, the strict regimen, the food one dislikes, the trainer obeyed as a physician, and at the end a broken arm, mouthfuls of dust, many stripes and defeat
Wesley's sting, that the moderns only have discovered that it is legal to do all this and more for an eternal crown than the Greeks did for a corruptible one
themes: they which run in a race
so run that ye may obtain

26.pericope_label: I therefore so run; I keep under my body, lest I be a castaway
debates: Whether the buffeting of the body is literal or figurative: Clarke takes the body itself for the enemy, to be mortified by self-denial, abstinence and severe labour and made the slave of the soul; Gill denies this expressly, that it means neither immoderate watchings and fastings nor whipping and scourging and lying on the bare ground, but the body of sin and the corruption of nature; Ellicott insists the language of the whole passage is figurative and refers not to inflicting pain but to subduing the appetites; Robertson denies the Gnostic premise that Paul thought his body evil; Calvin observes that the ancient monks meant to obey the precept literally and yet the main thing was wanting in them

What the adverb in the first verse means: Barnes takes it that Paul did not run without knowing what he aimed at; Clarke offers three senses together, uncertainly, since only one could win however many ran, ignorantly, as of a man who does not know the course, and without observation, since all eyes were on the runners and Paul knew his false brethren waited for his halting; Calvin reports a reading he does not adopt, that the words refer to full assurance of hope, preferring himself that the point is to direct the course straight so that it may not be wavering

What the last word means and what it proves: Ellicott says the common rendering castaway conveys a wrong impression, the Greek meaning rather one who has not behaved according to the prescribed regulations; Robertson finds the tone the important thing, a wholesome fear instead of smug complacency in the greatest of all heralds; Wesley presses it into doctrine, holding that this single text gives a just notion of election and reprobation, since believers are elected to privileges which if abused will leave those very elect persons reprobate, Paul himself being the instance
outliers: Clarke's third sense of the adverb, without observation, filled out from Paul's own situation, that his false brethren waited for his halting, the persecuting Jews and Gentiles longed for his downfall, and the Church looked on him with anxiety
Robertson's explanation of beating the air as the shadow-fighting a boxer practised without an opponent, with the remark that Paul smote something more solid than air
Gill's support for the sense of the verb from a story of Menedemus, so pugnacious in scholastic exercises that his opponents never departed without black eyes
Robertson's image, borrowed from Robertson and Plummer, of chariot horses which must be kept well in hand by whip and rein

Clarke's account of the herald's office at the games, that he proclaimed the conditions, displayed the prizes, exhorted the combatants, pronounced the names of the victors and set the crowns on their heads
Lightfoot's pursuit of the last word into the rabbinic vocabulary, matching it with the Hebrew terms for approved and not approved, fit and unfit
